Tech Scan: Maturity

How far to let an agent go, level by level. The ladder runs from writing every line yourself (L0) to a dark factory where you only step in by exception (L5). At every level the question is the same: what does a person still read, and when?

Draft research reference. Based on published research and practitioner accounts, not local deployment tests.

For the practices behind each level, read How the concepts fit together in Concepts.

Key points

  • Autonomy is a setting chosen per task and per deployment, not a property of a team or a tool. "Maturity" is the capability to choose and support a higher setting safely.
  • The ladder runs L0–L5 on Dan Shapiro's framing with Knight First Amendment Institute role names; verification is the gate at every climb.
  • Score per task and cap by risk; L5 is a direction, not a target — unattended autonomy suits exploration and throwaway work, not production defaults.

Where are we?

The five-levels framing[1] describes delegation distance: how much of the work an agent does before a person has to understand it. The Knight First Amendment Institute[4] adds the missing half — the human roles those levels produce: operator, collaborator, consultant, approver, observer. Addy Osmani's agentic autonomy levels[2] push the framing further: autonomy is a property of a deployment for a task, not of a person or a tool, and capability is something you grow deliberately through feedback loops. The AI Codebase Maturity Model[3] reaches a similar conclusion from a different direction: progress comes from tightening feedback loops, not from chasing a level.

So this page separates two things that maturity models often blur. The level is the autonomy setting for one task. Maturity is the team's capability to choose a higher setting for that task — and to support it — without losing the ability to detect and undo mistakes. A team can run L3 on one workflow and L1 on another; the Futurum analysis of Qodo's own L1–L4 earned-autonomy framework makes the same point in Qodo's numbering: "a team can operate at L4 for some workflows while keeping others at L3"[12].

Self-test. Pick the last three changes your team shipped. For each one, answer: what did a person read, and when? Every line? Every diff? Evidence of checks? Nothing until after release? The answers locate you on the ladder per task, not per team.

Running example, used across the playbook: Maya's small-business asset-management app. Handing the agent the handover-form wording change is an L2 task. Letting the agent redesign the reporting module from a spec — and read only the evidence — is an L3 or L4 task, and only if the verification underneath is real.

The ladder L0 to L5

The levels follow Dan Shapiro's five levels framing[1], extended with an explicit L0 baseline, and the role names follow the Knight First Amendment Institute[4]. Addy Osmani's levels[2] name the same progression differently — Assist, Supervised action, Scoped task delegation, Goal-driven autonomy, Parallel delegation, and Managed-by-exception orchestration — and argue that a single ladder cannot capture both how far one agent goes and how well many agents are coordinated. Numbers are not comparable across frameworks — treat them as a shared vocabulary for this page, not a universal scale.

Summary of the six levels: agent scope, what the person still reads, and the exit criterion for the next climb.
LevelName (role)Agent scopePerson still readsExit criterion
L0BaselineNo delegation; autocomplete at mostEvery line, as the authorDelegate three recurring chores to an agent on request
L1OperatorAgent helps on request inside granted toolsEvery line of small tasksAgent mode handles a real multi-file task and loops on test feedback
L2CollaboratorAgent edits code, runs tests, reworks within limitsEvery diff before it shipsA second agent or worktree runs in parallel and you read evidence, not lines
L3ConsultantSeveral agents run supervised, each with own branch and checksPRs and check evidence for each change, not linesThe agent starts work from triggers; you review specs, plans and test results instead of gating each change
L4ApproverPersistent agent starts work from triggers, plans and runs sessionsGoals, plans, exceptions, final evidenceAuthorised scope, holdout evaluation and minutes-fast rollback are proven
L5ObserverAuthorised automation can release without a readerOutcomes, by exceptionNo next level on this page — see the direction-not-target section

L0 — Baseline: you write every line

L0 is the no-agent baseline, included so the ladder has a floor. You write the code; an autocomplete suggestion is the most delegation. The exit criterion is behavioural, not technical: the working exit test is behavioural, not technical: delegate three recurring chores to an agent on request. Concepts that apply here: context engineering (what you paste into the prompt) and verification engineering (how you check your own work).

L1 — Operator: the agent helps when asked

The Knight role at L1 is operator: the person prompts, reviews, and remains accountable for every line. This matches Shapiro's "spicy autocomplete" — powerful suggestions, but the person is still the author. The Concepts that make this level useful rather than busywork: context engineering and harness engineering — Osmani's level 1 notes the agent's ceiling is set by the quality of context and tools you give it[2].

L2 — Collaborator: the agent does the typing, you read the diffs

At L2 the agent edits files, runs tests and reworks within agreed limits, and the person reviews every diff before it ships. The Knight role is collaborator. This is where loop engineering and verification engineering start to carry weight: the agent's rework loop is only as good as the checks it runs. The coding agents page covers which tools sit here; the harness page covers what keeps the loop bounded.

L3 — Consultant: supervise several agents, read the evidence

At L3 several agents run in parallel — separate worktrees, branches and check runs — and the person's job shifts from reading lines to supervising and reading evidence. The Knight role is consultant. This is the first level where the graph engineering and spec-driven development concepts become load-bearing: parallel agents need contracts for their work. Gametime's published example[13] scores this level per repository — its web and mobile apps at L3 while the backend stayed high L2 on Shapiro's framework — which is the per-task scoring this page recommends.

L4 — Approver: the agent starts work, you approve decisions

At L4 a persistent agent starts work from triggers — a schedule, an event, a message — plans the work, runs sessions and collects evidence. The Knight role is approver: the person sets goals, approves plans and decisions, and handles exceptions. This is where persistent agents, harness engineering and intent-driven development carry the load. The workflows and factories page covers the orchestration side; verification covers what must be independent before you stop reviewing every change.

L5 — Observer: outcomes by exception

At L5 an authorised automation route can carry a change to release without a person reading it first; the person watches outcomes and intervenes by exception. The Knight role is observer. Shapiro's March 2026 dark factories post describes StrongDM's Attractor — a feedback-loop factory explained by StrongDM's CTO Justin Massa — alongside Trycycle, Shapiro's own minimal skill[9]; the StrongDM account is a vendor self-description, not an independently verified benchmark. The Oversight Ladder[10] is explicit that this level suits "exploration and throwaway work, not production a business depends on". Concepts behind it: the software factory with light and dark routes, guardrails, and model selection.

Verification is the gate

Every climb on this ladder is gated by verification, and the requirement gets stricter as the person reads less. The rule the verification engineering concept already states applies here directly: nothing climbs past L2 without an automated check the agent cannot edit, and the climb from L4 to L5 additionally needs independent verification plus rollback measured in minutes. The verification scan covers how to build those checks; the Concepts section covers why they must be independent of the author.

Minimum check strength required before climbing to each level.
Climb toMinimum checkWhy
L1You can run the code and read what the agent suggestsThe person is still the author; the risk is wasted effort, not shipped defects
L2Automated tests exist and the agent runs them in its loopThe agent now types; the person reads diffs, so checks must catch what eyes miss
L3Checks are independent — the authoring agent cannot edit themParallel agents multiply the blast radius of a weak check
L4Independent verification, holdout evaluation, rollback in minutesThe agent starts work without a reader; detection and undo must not depend on attention
L5Authorised route, monitored exceptions, proven stop and rollbackNo reader is in the loop at all; the route itself must be the check

Addy Osmani frames the same gate as three questions to answer before raising autonomy on a task[2]:

  • How fast do we know we're wrong? Detection latency sets the ceiling on how much damage an autonomous run can do.
  • How cleanly can we undo it? Rollback that takes minutes permits autonomy; rollback that takes days does not.
  • What proves we're right? The check must be independent of the agent that produced the work.

The two plateaus

Two climbs fail for organisational reasons, not technical ones. Naming them helps teams diagnose a stall instead of blaming the tool.

L2 to L3: reviewer fatigue

At L2 the person reads every diff. The moment parallel agents multiply the diff volume, reading stops scaling — and teams quietly drift back to skimming, which is L3 behaviour without L3 verification. The exit criterion is therefore behavioural: you only climb when a second agent or worktree runs in parallel and you have replaced line-reading with evidence-reading that the authoring agent cannot edit. Anthropic's measurement work[8] shows the same shift in the wild: as agent autonomy rose through late 2025, the share of tool calls with a human in the loop fell to roughly 73%, and the length of uninterrupted agent runs grew sharply.

L3 to L4: spec quality and the coordination cliff

The harder plateau is L3 to L4. Steve Yegge's account, analysed by Augment Code[11], describes the coordination problems that appear when agents outnumber the humans who can supervise them — the coordination cliff. The climb depends on spec quality: if specs feed agents well enough that the agent starts work from triggers and you approve goals and exceptions instead of gating each change, you are at L4; if you still review every change, you are at L3. Dan Shapiro's March 2026 dark factories post[9] names the same prerequisite from the other side — his Trycycle skill is the plan-check loop in its plainest form: define the problem, write a plan, implement, check, repeat.

Worked example. Gametime publishes per-repository levels: web and mobile at L3, backend at high L2 on Shapiro's framework[13]. That is the pattern to copy — score per task and per repo, cap by risk, and let different parts of the system sit at different levels.

Score per task, cap by risk

A team does not have a level; a task does. The Futurum analysis of Qodo's L1–L4 earned-autonomy framework says the same in Qodo's numbering: "a team can operate at L4 for some workflows while keeping others at L3"[12]. The METR study[6] of 16 developers on 246 tasks adds a warning about measurement: developers' own estimates of how much the agent sped them up were far more optimistic than observed completion times — so score tasks on observable behaviours (what the person read, which checks ran, whether rollback was needed), not on self-reported velocity.

Before raising autonomy on a task, write the run contract. Osmani's checklist[2] covers:

  • Goal — the outcome, in one sentence.
  • Scope — which files, services and systems the agent may touch.
  • Non-goals — what the agent must not do, even if it sees a way.
  • Tools and permissions — exactly what the agent can run and change.
  • Stopping condition — when the agent must stop and ask.
  • Evidence — what the agent must produce to prove the work.
  • Escalation — who decides when the agent is unsure.
  • Budget — time, tokens and cost ceiling for the run.

Then cap by risk. Osmani's metrics for judging whether autonomy is working[2]: mean time between interventions, longest unattended run, defect escape rate, and token cost per accepted change. If interventions cluster, the level is too high for that task; step down.

What the delivery system must support

The organisational axis matters as much as the task axis. The 2025 DORA report[5], based on roughly 5,000 professionals, found that AI adoption is associated with worse delivery stability unless the surrounding system is strong — "AI doesn't fix a team; it amplifies what's already there". DORA names seven capabilities that magnify AI's benefits: clear AI stance, healthy data ecosystems, strong version control, small batch sizes, platform engineering, quality internal platforms, and fast feedback loops. The transformation page covers building those capabilities; the short version for this ladder is that your delivery system caps the level any task can safely reach. Weak version control or slow feedback makes L3 the ceiling no matter how good the agent is. The delivery scan covers the release and rollback side of that cap.

L5: a direction, not a target

L5 is the level most easily misread as a destination. Three cautions:

  • Vendor self-description. The best-known L5 account is StrongDM's Attractor factory, explained by its CTO in Shapiro's March 2026 dark factories post[9]. That is one company's account of its own system — useful as a pattern, not as evidence that L5 is proven at scale.
  • Unattended autonomy has a domain. The Oversight Ladder[10] is explicit: Level 5 is for "exploration and throwaway work, not production a business depends on", and "treating Level 5 as the goal is how expensive mistakes reach production".
  • No proven general playbook. There is no public, independently verified playbook for climbing from L4 to L5. The Yegge analysis[11] describes the coordination problems at the top of the ladder; it does not hand over a recipe.

Treat L5 as the direction the ladder points — useful for designing guardrails, routes and monitoring now — rather than a level to announce. The software factory concept's light and dark routes are the same idea from the release side: dark routes are where L5 behaviour lives, and they stay dark until the evidence says otherwise.

Step back down

Maturity is not a ratchet. The Concepts page already states the regression rule: "If incidents or undone changes become more common, restore human review." Operationally, that means:

  • Track the Osmani metrics per task type; a rising intervention rate or defect escape rate is the signal to lower the setting for that task.
  • Keep the run contract current — scope, stopping condition and escalation paths decay as the codebase changes.
  • Remember Fowler's caution about maturity models: the true outcome of an assessment "isn't what level you are but the list of things you need to work on to improve"[7]. A level is a diagnostic, not a badge.

  1. Dan Shapiro, The Five Levels: from Spicy Autocomplete to the Dark Factory — five-level delegation framing; the ladder names and exit tests are this page's synthesis.
  2. Addy Osmani, Agentic Autonomy Levels — autonomy as a per-deployment setting, three questions, run-contract checklist, autonomy metrics.
  3. Daniel Vaughan, The AI Codebase Maturity Model — levels defined by feedback-loop topology; three-axis assessment (autonomy, controls, governance).
  4. Knight First Amendment Institute, Levels of Autonomy for AI Agents — operator, collaborator, consultant, approver, observer roles.
  5. Google Cloud, Announcing the 2025 DORA Report — AI amplifies teams; seven capabilities; stability findings.
  6. METR, Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity — 16 developers, 246 tasks; self-reports vs observed time.
  7. Martin Fowler, MaturityModel (bliki) — maturity models as diagnostics, not badges.
  8. Anthropic, Measuring Agent Autonomy — human-in-loop share and run lengths over time.
  9. Dan Shapiro, Dark Factories: Rise of the Trycycle — StrongDM's Attractor (CTO account) and Shapiro's Trycycle skill; vendor self-description.
  10. dominik_ddd, The Oversight Ladder: The Five Levels of AI Coding Autonomy — dial not scoreboard; Level 5 domain limits.
  11. Augment Code, Steve Yegge's 8 Levels of AI Development — eight-level progression and coordination problems at the top.
  12. Futurum Group, Qodo Builds the Governance Layer Agentic SDLC Has Been Missing — Qodo's L1–L4 earned autonomy framework; per-workflow levels.
